profiles.meeting_scenario: San Diego State University's biomedical engineering program is holding a design review of its revised graduate elective, 'Medical Device Design through Design Control,' before the next spring offering. The specific proposal under review updates the existing challenge-based course by keeping the cardiovascular and orthopedic device challenges but changing how students document design controls, conduct field immersion, and pass stage-gate reviews. The agenda is to assess whether the proposed course package is ready for departmental approval, identify any gaps in realism or compliance framing, and decide what revisions are needed before the syllabus and teaching materials are finalized. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the revised course structure, with both participants believing they have aligned on what must be included in the final course package.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Course Director and Associate Professor of Biomedical Engineering
members.expertise: Challenge-based learning, medical device prototyping, design pedagogy, student assessment
members.background: Dr. Marquez has led the medical device design course for four years and previously worked in an academic med-tech incubator supporting student teams developing early-stage cardiovascular and orthopedic concepts.
members.private_state: She wants the redesign approved quickly so the course can be advertised on time, while preserving the hands-on, immersive character that students consistently praise; she is also trying to keep the documentation burden manageable enough that student teams still have time to do meaningful design work.
hidden_assumptions: A 'design review' in a course setting is primarily a structured critique that helps students reflect and improve, not a simulation of a formal industry phase-gate with independence requirements.
A 'complete DHF' for grading means a coherent set of major design-control artifacts showing traceability and rationale, even if signatures, document histories, and closed action logs are lightweight.

The longstanding educational relationship with the university hospital means students can do limited follow-up clarification with clinicians after the initial immersion as long as no patient identifiers are discussed.
When colleagues refer to 'the ortho module from last year,' they usually mean the simplified tibial tray fatigue challenge that students found teachable and well-scoped.

members.name: Ravi Patel
members.role: Adjunct Lecturer in Regulatory Affairs and Industry Design Quality Advisor
members.expertise: FDA design controls, quality systems, medical device documentation, design transfer readiness
members.background: Patel spent twelve years in quality and regulatory roles at orthopedic and cardiovascular device companies and now advises university programs on making device-development training more industry-realistic.
members.private_state: He wants the course to look credibly aligned with FDA design-control practice so it can be showcased to industry partners and internship sponsors; he is especially concerned about students learning habits that would be unacceptable in a real quality system.
hidden_assumptions: A 'design review' should model a formal documented review with named inputs, outputs, action items, and reviewers who are not the design team itself, otherwise students learn the wrong norm.
A 'complete DHF' implies document control discipline, including revision status, dated approvals, and explicit disposition of open issues, even in an educational simulation.
Clinical immersion for a course should stop at the approved observation event, with any later questions routed through scheduled faculty-mediated sessions rather than informal clinician follow-ups.

When someone says 'the ortho module from last year,' they are referring to the revised post-market complaint case that was circulated among faculty over the summer, not the older tibial tray fatigue challenge.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that each student team should have a formal 'design review' before design freeze.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a faculty-led checkpoint where teams present their user needs, concepts, and rationale, receive critique, and then revise their documents.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a simulated industry phase-gate with defined review inputs/outputs, written action items, and at least one reviewer who is independent of the student team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design-control discussion, 'design review' sounds like an unambiguous best practice, so both treat the phrase as settled and move on without unpacking how formal or independent the review must be.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'DHF complete' means for the course package
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that students should submit a 'complete DHF' as the main graded deliverable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a pedagogically complete package containing the major artifacts—user needs, design inputs, concepts, risk analysis, verification planning, and traceability—sufficient to demonstrate learning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a quality-system-complete package with controlled revisions, dated approvals, resolved review actions, and a cleaner audit trail that mirrors real design history expectations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both value documentation and use the same FDA terminology, the difference hides inside their threshold for completeness rather than in the visible structure of the deliverable.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of clinician follow-up after immersion
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the revised course should preserve 'field immersion' and let students refine needs after the clinical visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes students may send follow-up clarification questions to participating clinicians after the observation day, as has informally happened in prior offerings under the standing educational arrangement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the only approved clinical contact is the scheduled immersion event itself, and that any later refinement will come from guest lectures or faculty-mediated summaries rather than direct clinician exchanges.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither person sees the underlying access rule as a design topic worth restating; they each think the operational constraints around immersion are already known from prior course planning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'ortho module from last year' is being carried forward
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to keep 'the ortho module from last year' with minor cleanup.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the older tibial tray fatigue challenge built around design inputs, material constraints, and benchtop verification planning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the newer post-market complaint and instrument-usability case that a faculty working group circulated as the planned orthopedic update.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both versions are legitimately associated with last year's orthopedic content, and the shorthand phrase feels specific enough that neither person suspects they are picturing different teaching cases.

turns.inner_thought: I need this locked today so we can advertise on schedule. The core structure is already proven: the cardiovascular challenge plus the tibial tray fatigue orthopedic case students handled well last year. If Ravi is comfortable with that backbone, I can make only light revisions and avoid reopening the whole course.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Ravi. What I'd like to do today is confirm that the revised course is basically ready for spring. My intent is to keep the cardiovascular challenge and the ortho module from last year as the backbone, then make sure the updated design-control pieces fit cleanly around them.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Keeping the orthopedic complaint case will make this feel much more credible to industry partners, especially if we tighten the quality framing around it. If the underlying cases stay familiar, I can push harder on the documentation habits without sounding like I'm asking for a full rebuild.
turns.utterance: Overall, I think the structure is strong. Keeping the ortho module from last year should help with continuity, and it gives us a good platform for making the design-control framing feel more industry-realistic.

turns.inner_thought: I want one meaningful checkpoint before freeze, not a bureaucratic exercise. The value is faculty critique that helps teams sharpen needs, concepts, and rationale while there's still time to improve. If I say 'design review,' he'll hear what he expects, and I can still keep it efficient enough that the course remains hands-on.
turns.utterance: One key element I want to preserve is that each team has a design review before design freeze. That gives us a clean checkpoint for targeted feedback without slowing the pace of the challenge too much.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, as long as it really behaves like a gate and not just an informal coaching session. Students need to see that a design review produces documented outcomes, action items, and a basis for moving ahead. If we capture it cleanly, they'll internalize the right norm.
turns.utterance: I like that. If the design review output is captured cleanly, students will experience it as a proper gate before they move forward, which is exactly the right habit to build.

turns.inner_thought: The DHF should stay the main graded package, but in a course-appropriate sense: major artifacts, visible traceability, clear rationale. I do not want students drowning in signatures and version minutiae instead of actually designing. Templates can carry enough structure without turning this into paperwork theater.
turns.utterance: For the deliverables, the main graded artifact would still be a complete DHF. I’m planning to use templates that make it easier for teams to show traceability across needs, inputs, risks, and verification planning.

turns.inner_thought: That's the right anchor, provided 'complete DHF' really means something reviewable like it would in a quality system. I want students to keep it current, with enough discipline that an outside person could inspect it midstream and understand status, revisions, and what still needs disposition.
turns.utterance: I agree—a complete DHF is the right anchor. It would be especially useful if students learn to keep that package reviewable at any point in the semester rather than treating it as something assembled at the end.

turns.inner_thought: I need to protect the clinical exposure; it's one of the best parts of the course. Students always write better needs once they've seen the setting and had a chance to ask a few follow-up clarification questions afterward. We’ve done that informally before under the hospital relationship, and it keeps the projects grounded.
turns.utterance: The other piece I’m keen to preserve is field immersion. Students refine their needs statements much better once they’ve had the clinical visit and a chance to follow up on what they saw.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely keep the observation component, but we need to keep the boundaries clean. The debrief and any faculty-mediated clarification should be enough; I do not want students normalizing informal clinician contact after the approved session. Still, no need to make that a big detour here if we're aligned on preserving field immersion.
turns.utterance: I agree that field immersion is important. If the debrief after the observation is set up well, students should have enough material to refine needs safely and keep the learning value of that experience.

turns.inner_thought: The orthopedic case works because it's teachable early: students can derive design inputs from the problem, weigh constraints, and plan benchtop verification without getting lost in a giant systems problem. That's exactly why I want to keep the tibial tray challenge in the sequence.
turns.utterance: And from a sequencing standpoint, the orthopedic challenge is still a very manageable way to teach design inputs, risk tradeoffs, and verification planning early in the term.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the complaint-based ortho case naturally shows why review records and DHF discipline matter. When students see how post-market issues connect back to earlier decisions, they understand why stronger gates and cleaner files are not just bureaucracy. This is exactly the module industry people will recognize.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The orthopedic case is also useful because complaint-handling logic naturally leads students into why stronger review records matter, and it reinforces the value of a complete DHF and a solid design review rhythm.

turns.inner_thought: I can tighten templates and expectations a bit to satisfy him, but I have to protect bandwidth for actual design work. If teams spend all semester polishing forms, the course loses what makes it effective. As long as the design review and complete DHF are there in a sensible educational form, we should be fine.
turns.utterance: I can certainly tighten the templates a bit. I just want to avoid overwhelming teams with paperwork, as long as the design review and the complete DHF are both in place and doing the work we need pedagogically.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds workable. If she cleans up the packet and preserves the immersion and gate structure, I can support approval and present this as a credible design-controls course. I may still want the final materials to reflect stronger quality discipline, but I don't think I need to slow the approval today.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable to me. With field immersion retained and the design review built in, I think the course is in good shape for approval once the packet gets cleaned up.
